newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian opposition leader to miss London talks.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian opposition leader to miss London talks.

text.p: A Nigerian opposition leader on Wednesday accused the military government of sabotaging his plans to travel to London to discuss Nigeria's woes with a Commonwealth group.

Abraham Adesanya, deputy chairman of the umbrella National Democratic Coalition (NADECO), whose passport was seized by state security agents in 1994, told a news conference he got it back on Wednesday only to discover that it had expired.
Adesanya was to lead a NADECO delegation to a meeting with the Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) in London on Thursday and Friday.
"I personally believe that they chose to release the passport knowing I could not travel with it," he said.
Nigeria has protested against the meeting, saying the Commonwealth -- grouping Britain and its former colonies -- risked breaking up over its stand on Nigeria.

"The hostile attitude and the use of bodies like CMAG against my country and developing countries contains the seeds of future disintegration of the Commonwealth," Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi told diplomats at a meeting in the capital Abuja on Tuesday.

"It is the expectation of Nigeria that the meeting will understand the implications of what it is about to do at its London meeting," he said, reading from the text of protest letters he has sent to the chairman of CMAG, Zimbabwean Foreign Minister Stan Mudenge.

Adesanya said he tried to renew the passport in Lagos but was told by the passport officer that his name was on a list of those who could not be issued the travel document without clearance from security authorities the capital Abuja.
"It shows that they have something to hide which they don't want us to reveal," Adesanya said.
CMAG was set up at the 1995 Commonwealth summit in Auckland, New Zealand, where Nigeria was suspended for hanging nine minority rights activists including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa.
It is made up of Britain, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Ghana, Jamaica and Malaysia, and it is due to recommend whether Nigeria should remain suspended.
Britain's Foreign Secretary has already said London would recommend that Nigeria should remain suspended.
Ikimi said Nigeria felt CMAG could no longer be impartial in its recommendations.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation, plunged into political turmoil in June 1993 when the army annulled a presidential election in spite of pledges to restore democracy.

Military ruler General Sani Abacha has promised to hand over to a democratically elected president in 1998. But the opposition is sceptical that this will happen and points to the continued detention of opponents -- among them Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled poll.
NADECO said in a statement that it would tell CMAG that the transition to civil rule programme being run by the military "is nothing but a fraud meant to perpetuate Abacha in governance."
It wants the release of all political prisoners and a restoration of the annulled vote.
